Gap compares a suburb's median with the sales-weighted median of its 12 nearest suburbs (within 25 km) in the same year. Rising suburbs with a big gap are the strongest leads.

How the numbers are worked out
  • Source: NSW Valuer General property sales, residential (primary purpose "Residence") sales from 2016 to 11 Nov 2026, $100k–$40M. Duplicate records and multi-lot sales are removed. 2026 is year to date.
  • Today's dollars: each year's prices are scaled by Sydney All groups CPI (ABS) to September 2026 levels, e.g. 2016 prices × 1.37, 2021 × 1.25, 2025 × 1.05. Sydney CPI is used for all of NSW, as ABS publishes no regional CPI. The value gap is unaffected; the 3-year change becomes a real change.
  • Houses are non-strata sales; units are strata lots (apartments, townhouses and villas on strata).
  • Median price is per suburb and calendar year. Suburbs need the minimum number of sales you set to appear.
  • Value gap = suburb median ÷ sales-weighted median price of its 12 nearest suburbs within 25 km (counting those with at least 5 sales, so busy towns outweigh small rural localities) − 1. Negative means cheaper than the surrounding area: a lead to investigate, not a valuation. Big blocks, rural fringes, water views and housing mix all move it.
  • Land $ per m² = price ÷ lot size for house sales on 100–4,000 m² lots.
  • Suburb locations are centroids from the Australian postcodes dataset (matched on suburb and postcode). Regions are ABS SA4 areas. Faint lines are NSW suburb (locality) boundaries; the coastline combines Natural Earth and those boundaries, lightly smoothed.
  • Watch for one-off development-site sales in small samples (e.g. new release areas); raise the minimum sales to filter them.

Data: NSW Valuer General property sales to 11 Nov 2026; ABS Sydney CPI to Sep 2026; suburb boundaries from NSW localities; coastline from Natural Earth. Exported 24 Nov 2026.
